## What to build

The thing a terminal cannot do at all: **the screenshots the agent looked at appear in the feed.**
An image the agent read renders inline at usable width, so a visual debugging loop can be followed
by scrolling rather than by opening files.

The correctness requirement is the whole ticket. Agents routinely re-render the same screenshot
path several times within one turn, so **each image row must show the bytes the agent saw at that
moment.** Three reads of the same filename are three different pictures, not the same picture three
times.

That fixes the source order. The **transcript's embedded bytes** are the primary source, since they
are what the agent actually saw and they cannot be invalidated later. The **file on disk** is a
fallback only, used when no embedded block exists, and it renders at the **lower tier** with a
visible label along the lines of "current file, not necessarily what the agent saw". Path-based
rendering as the primary source would silently show the wrong pixels in exactly the loop this
feature exists to support, which is worse than showing nothing.

# Worktree mechanics

Implementation work runs in a git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, never the shared main
checkout — multiple agent sessions run concurrently, and isolating each unit of work on its own
tree and branch keeps them from clobbering each other's files. A `PreToolUse` hook
(`scripts/worktree-guard.mjs`) enforces it, blocking agent `Edit`/`Write` to `apps/**` or
`packages/**` from outside a worktree; this file is the *how* it cites — naming, resuming an
interrupted worktree, recovering a deleted one. It applies to all implementation work, not just
`/implement` runs, and is self-contained so it stands alone when the hooks copy it into a
consumer project.

# Comment Discipline

Comments are a liability: they drift from the code and nobody re-verifies them
on every edit the way tests and types get re-verified. Default to NO comment.
Good code and good names are the documentation. Binds `//`, `/* */`, and `#`
alike, in every language in the repo.

## The one sanctioned comment: WHY the code cannot say

A comment earns its place only when it encodes a WHY that cannot be recovered by
reading the code itself:

- a constraint or invariant the code must honor (a version ceiling, an ordering
  requirement, a fail-closed contract)
- a workaround, paired with the reason it exists (the bug/limitation it routes around)
- a choice that looks wrong on first read but is deliberate

If the WHY becomes inferable from the code (a rename, a type, an assertion makes
it obvious) — delete the comment. It's now drift risk, not documentation.
